vignette:
Daniel Makoa had built his life around books, meetings, and the steady rituals of publishing in Sydney, but a single night had rearranged the way the world felt to him. Years earlier, during a man-made disaster at a crowded venue where a sudden violent disturbance and the smell of spilled alcohol marked the start of chaos, he had been trapped long enough to take in details he could not later forget: the hard shine of the floor, people rushing in fragments, the angle of a doorway that seemed to offer escape and then did not. From the beginning, what stayed with him was not a blurred impression but a sequence of vivid, detailed images that arrived with such force that he felt he was back there for a moment, seeing it in pictures rather than words. He would try to talk about it with his wife or a doctor, and even the act of describing it would pull the memory forward, making his chest tighten as if the scene had reached up and taken hold of him again. He had come to believe that if the images were so clear, so insistently available, then the danger must still be near enough to matter.

In the months afterward, Daniel began shaping his life around that certainty. He stopped seeing friends as often, telling himself he was busy, though the deeper reason was that social meals, bars, and casual gatherings carried the risk of an alcohol smell that could abruptly drag him back to the night of the disaster. At restaurants or work functions, he would choose a seat with his back against the wall so he could see the room, and once inside any space he found himself constantly scanning doorways, reflections, and the faces of strangers for signs that something was about to go wrong. These habits made him feel momentarily safer, yet they also kept the event close at hand; every careful survey of the room seemed to confirm that he was right to stay guarded, and the more he arranged his body and attention around escape routes, the more the memory sharpened. He found that the frightening event was most likely to surge into mind when he was not wanting it to, especially after a poor night’s sleep or after a nightmare that left him waking with the scene still clinging to him. In those half-dazed mornings, the images came back with a force that made him replay them, and each replay seemed to deepen their clarity.

By then he was on guard even inside his own home. Daniel moved through the house as though something might still break through the ordinary quiet, and ordinary sounds made him jump: a cupboard shutting, a car backfiring outside, his phone buzzing on the table. He felt jumpy in a way that embarrassed him, yet he could not relax. That constant sense of being under threat made the world feel as if it required more vigilance, and the more he watched and listened, the more his mind stayed tuned to danger. The same scanning that helped him keep watch also fed the memory; each time he checked the room or sat rigidly against the wall, he was reminded of the original chaos and the helplessness he had felt there. And because he was always bracing himself, every startle seemed to prove that the danger might return at any moment.

At work, Daniel still came into the publishing office, but he had become less spontaneous, less willing to linger with colleagues over lunch or attend evening events. His occupation, once a place of conversation and exchange, now felt like a series of settings to manage carefully. He noticed that even talking about the event in a staff meeting or with close friends could set off the same cascade: the images would enter his mind, vivid and unwanted, and afterward he would avoid further discussion, retreating from people and sitting himself where he could watch the room. The arrangements offered short-lived relief, but they also kept him trapped in the same posture of watchfulness, and his wife had begun to notice how rarely he fully let his guard down at home. He finally sought help when the nights became harder to bear—when he woke from nightmares already on edge, startled by small sounds in the house, and felt no part of his day was untouched by the need to scan, avoid, and prepare for danger. What he most hoped for was the chance to sleep without dread and to sit in a room, even his own living room, without feeling that he had to watch every corner. What frightened him most was the sense that the event had not stayed in the past at all, and that his mind would keep forcing him back into it.
